title: Ridgway Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Ridgway wells have a 184-foot median depth, 12 gpm median yield, and fractured-bedrock drilling costs of $65-$100 per foot.
h1: What Ridgway Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Buying land around Ridgway means evaluating more than whether a permit exists. The local record shows a mountain-bedrock setting where neighboring wells can differ substantially in depth, water level, and construction details. Within 5 miles of Ridgway, Colorado, DWR records include 510 permitted wells, although only 321 report a total depth and 141 report a pump yield.

This page uses those records to give you a practical starting point for a purchase, a new homesite, or a drilling budget. The strongest local pattern is favorable well production overall, paired with fractured granite and gneiss that can make any individual location unpredictable.

sections.heading: Ridgway well depth depends on fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Ridgway is 184 feet. The middle half runs from 85 to 300 feet, so a driller bidding a typical homesite will usually need to allow for a fairly broad range rather than quote one standard depth. The 90th percentile is 405 feet, while the deepest record reaches 4421 feet.

Depths are distributed across the area: 29% are under 100 feet, 42% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 25% between 300 and 600 feet, and 4% exceed 600 feet. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Dakota Sandstone and Dakota appear on a smaller number of permits, and no wells are identified in the Denver Basin aquifer.

sections.heading: Most Ridgway wells make useful household water
sections.html:
Among the 141 local records reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 8.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a solid local production pattern for a household well, but it is not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot or a particular bedrock fracture.

Yield records show 43% above 15 gallons per minute, 45% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 11% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 1% under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for a production test and the well-completion report. A Colorado exempt household-use well also has a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit, even when the well could produce more.

sections.heading: Water levels around Ridgway vary by location
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median depth of 56 feet. The middle half ranges from 9 to 121 feet below ground surface. That spread is wide enough to affect pump setting, trenching, storage, and the cost of getting water into a house.

Only 28 wells report a static water level, so this dataset is not large enough to establish a dependable decade-by-decade water-table trend. Do not treat the median as a guarantee for a vacant parcel. Nearby well logs, the proposed well elevation, and a driller’s local experience are more useful for estimating where water may stand on your property.

sections.heading: Ridgway permit history shows steady drilling activity
sections.html:
Permit activity began in the local record in the 1950s, with 5 permits that decade, and continued through the newest permit year, 2025. The largest decade was the 1990s with 103 permits. The record also shows 72 in the 1980s, 72 in the 2000s, 53 in the 1970s, 53 in the 2010s, 32 in the 2020s, and 1 in the 1960s.

Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth) appears most often, with 110 records. Mccracken Well Drilling Inc (Mccracken, Alan E.) appears on 36, and Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.) on 30. These names are useful when comparing nearby completion histories around Loghill Village, Portland, Ouray, and Colona, but old records do not replace a current site evaluation.

sections.heading: A Ridgway well budget starts with the rock
sections.html:
Local drilling is modeled as fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65-$100 per foot. At the 184-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone is estimated at about $12,000-$18,400.

A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $18,000-$30,400 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, or a low-producing fracture can push the actual bid higher. Have the proposal state what is included, including mobilization, casing, grout, pump equipment, storage, testing, trenching, and electrical work. Compare bids on the same scope rather than on footage alone.

sections.heading: Check water quality, yield, septic, and the homesite
sections.html:
Water quantity is only one part of due diligence. Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental inventory includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 81 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination at a specific parcel, but they are reasons to review site history and test the finished well before relying on it.

Low-yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured rock even though the local yield records are generally favorable. Confirm the proposed well location can be separated from septic components, buildings, driveways, and property lines under the applicable requirements. A septic designer should evaluate soil and slope before you commit to a house plan. Water rights, DWR permitting, and an augmentation plan may also matter, especially in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Use neighboring Ridgway wells before buying or building
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and the closest completed wells. Compare depths, aquifer descriptions, casing and grout, pump yields, static water levels, and well elevations. The local median is useful for budgeting, but the 85-to-300-foot middle range shows why a single nearby well should not be treated as a guaranteed result.

For a purchase near Ridgway, Loghill Village, or the Ouray side of the valley, make water testing, well-flow information, and septic feasibility part of your review period. For a new build, get a driller’s site-specific estimate and confirm access for equipment before finalizing the homesite. Colorado permits and an exempt-well limitation do not by themselves promise adequate household water.

faq.q: How deep are wells near Ridgway, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth within 5 miles of Ridgway is 184 feet. The middle half runs from 85 to 300 feet, while the 90th percentile is 405 feet. About 29% are under 100 feet and 42% are between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make the depth at a specific lot unpredictable.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Ridgway?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $65-$100 per foot. At the 184-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $12,000-$18,400. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $18,000-$30,400. Access, casing, grout, greater depth, and difficult rock can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Ridgway?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 8.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. About 43% of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 1% are under 1 gallon per minute. A production test is still necessary because bedrock fractures vary from lot to lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Ridgway?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles are 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 81 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test a completed well for site-appropriate contaminants, review local history, and retest if land use or water quality changes.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Ridgway?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, construction report, yield test, static water level, casing and grout details, and the closest neighboring wells. The local static-water median is 56 feet, but the middle half ranges from 9 to 121 feet. Also confirm septic feasibility, access, water rights, and whether an augmentation plan is required.
